chapter_theme: Courtesy of character, பண்பு, is what makes one fully human and keeps the world going. It reaches even to enemies, begins in being approachable, and without it sharp intelligence and great wealth come to nothing.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: how one comes to have it (991-992), the eminence of those who do (993-996), and the lowness of those who don't (997-1000). 1000 also introduces the next chapter on useless wealth.

991.reading: They say the practice called courtesy is easy to reach through being accessible to everyone.
991.nuance: வழக்கு makes courtesy a public custom, not an inner trait. Being available turns out to be the whole method, and யார்மாட்டும் gives it no exception. Parimelazhagar calls it something that wins over the whole world, which adds a strategic note.

992.reading: Love and being born in a seasoned family: these two are the way called courtesy.
992.nuance: This puts birth among courtesy's sources. Parimelazhagar softens it, saying குடிப்பிறத்தல் here means the conduct of those so born, and neither factor suffices alone. Kalaignar goes further, asking only that one have the marks of such birth.

993.reading: Likeness of limbs isn't likeness among people; true likeness is likeness of settled character.
993.nuance: வெறுத்தக்க usually means hateful, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as செறியத்தக்க, 'to be drawn close', which is what makes the line work. Pope's gloss, 'qualities that attract', follows him. I can't confirm this sense from the verse alone.

positions.position: The issue is likeness to good people: bodily likeness doesn't amount to that, because the body doesn't last and character does.
positions.quote: செறியத்தகாத உடம்பால் ஒத்தல் ஒருவனுக்கு நன்மக்களோடு ஒப்பாகாமையின்

positions.position: The issue is membership of humankind: those without good character shouldn't be counted as people.

994.reading: The world honours the character of those whose useful lives come from doing good with fairness.
994.nuance: The world honours the பண்பு, not the deeds or their outcome, which makes deeds evidence of character. Parimelazhagar says that it is useful to oneself and to others alike.

995.reading: Scorn hurts even in jest, so those who know how others feel have courtesy even in enmity.
995.nuance: Parimelazhagar insists that the two clauses are one argument, and criticizes others who read them apart: knowing that scorn hurts is the reason for courtesy. பாடு here is what another person undergoes.

996.reading: The world exists by resting upon those of courtesy; otherwise it would enter the earth and perish.
996.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes உலகம் here the way of the world, not the planet. Kalaignar makes it a should: worldly practices ought to depend on such people. A claim about reality becomes a recommendation.

997.reading: Even though sharp as a file, those without human courtesy are like trees.
997.nuance: The chime of அரம் and மரம் has the point in it. Parimelazhagar says the file wears down what it touches without wearing itself, and the tree has only one sense. Intelligence used without courtesy isn't merely inadequate, it is destructive.

998.reading: Failing in courtesy, even toward those who act without friendship and without kindness, is lowness.
998.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is reflexive: respond in kind and you become like them. The insult harms the character of the one who returns it.

999.reading: For those who aren't capable of laughing, the great wide world lies in darkness even in the daytime.
999.nuance: Laughter is treated as a skill (வல்லர்), and the lack of it as blindness. Parimelazhagar makes it the joy of mingling, and says such people don't understand the world because they can't mix with it. He reports a variant reading too.

1000.reading: Great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel.
1000.nuance: Wealth is good milk here, and the fault is the holder's alone. பெற்ற, 'obtained', suggests to Parimelazhagar that he couldn't have created it himself.

links.note: The same three words meet. 871 calls enmity the thing that has no பண்பு, not to be wanted even in jest. 995 says that those who know others' feelings have பண்பு even within enmity. Enmity is by definition devoid of courtesy, and yet courtesy can survive inside it.
993 says that likeness of limbs isn't human likeness, and 1071 gives the unsettling result: the base look exactly like people. The chapter on baseness starts where this verse ends.
Both call a person a tree for a moral lack: 997 for lacking human courtesy, 576 for having eyes without kindly regard. Each states a difference between being human and being merely alive.

Consecutive chapters end by making the world depend on a moral elite: if the worthy decline the earth can't carry its load (990), and without the courteous the world sinks into it (996). Two images of ground failing.

Both judge wealth by where it lands. In 216 wealth in the hands of the kind is a fruit tree in the village, and in 1000 wealth in the discourteous spoils in its vessel. The next chapter's 1008 completes the set with a poisonous tree.

972 denies that birth settles distinction, and 992, two chapters later, places birth among courtesy's two sources. Parimelazhagar's gloss, which turns birth into conduct, can be seen as a way of closing the gap.
386 says that the land extols a king easy to see and not harsh in speech. 991 gives ordinary people the same recipe. Accessibility is a virtue at every scale in the Kural.

786 distinguishes the laugh of the face from the laugh of the heart in friendship. Parimelazhagar takes 999's laughter as inner joy in others' company, so a failure of that capacity darkens the world and not merely a friendship.

source_issues: 994: the Tamil in kural.jsonl begins யனொடு, but the commentaries show the opening word is நயனொடு, so the first syllable is missing.

991, 993, 994, 995, 997, 998, 999, 1000: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss, so it may not be independent. It was not used as a separate voice in this chapter.
993: Pope's gloss has 'souls' for மக்கள், a term that is not in the verse.
